chunks: From him, from Ayyub ibn Nuḥ, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from whoever narrated to him, from Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) who said:

A woman came to ʿUmar asking him about her divorce. He said, 'Go to this man and ask him,' meaning ʿAlī (peace be upon him). She said to ʿAlī (peace be upon him), 'My husband has divorced me.' He said, 'Did you wash your private part?' She returned to ʿUmar and said, 'He sent me to a man who plays (is joking).' He said, 'I sent you to him twice,' every time she returned saying, 'He plays.' He said, 'Go to him, for he is the most knowledgeable of us.' He said, and ʿAlī (peace be upon him) said to her, 'Did you wash your private part?' She said, 'No.' He said, 'Then your husband has more right to your private part as long as you have not washed your private part.'

The explanation in these two narrations and what came in their meaning is that they are not repelled by the preceding narrations, because the explanation in them is that we carry them on a type of taqiyyah (dissimulation) or on the manner of attributing the opinion to them, so the saying of Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) 'ʿAlī (peace be upon him) said' means 'These people say that,' not that he was informing in reality about the opinion of the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him). And Abū Jaʿfar (peace be upon him) explicitly stated in the narration of Zurārah and others what is a refutation of it, and his saying 'They lied about ʿAlī (peace be upon him).' And if the matter is as we have said, then there is no contradiction between the narrations.
ai.seo_question: How is the apparent contradiction in ʿAlī's statement regarding divorce and washing resolved in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (a) clarifies that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib’s instruction to wash the private part before the third divorce was likely an expression of *taqiyyah* or reflecting the prevailing opinion of the people, rather than a strict legal condition for the divorce to take effect. This interpretation, supported by Imam al-Baqir’s (a) confirmation that the people lied about ʿAlī’s stance, resolves apparent contradictions with other hadiths by distinguishing between practical caution and definitive jurisprudence.
